knowledgeChecks.prompt: A counselor has simultaneous requests for a classroom lesson, routine schedule change, and a student with an immediate safety concern. How should work be prioritized?
choices: Address crisis risk first under protocol, then sequence urgent student needs and routine tasks in order.
Handle each request strictly in the chronological order it arrived so triage stays neutral and predictable.
Postpone planned classroom lessons and routine duties indefinitely whenever crisis demands appear busy.
Ask a trained peer helper to sit with the student in crisis while the counselor completes the lesson first.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Triage protects safety while transparent priorities, backup procedures, documentation, and follow-up keep the rest of the program functioning.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A large caseload limits access to individual counseling. Which management response is most appropriate?
choices: Place each referred student onto an open-ended individual counseling waitlist until an appointment opens.
Use needs and time data to balance tiered services, build referral pathways, and advocate for staffing.
Drop classroom lessons and small groups so the counselor’s full week goes to reactive individual crises.
See students strictly on a first-come basis without triaging urgency, need severity, or tiered alternatives.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: A comprehensive program uses multiple delivery modes, ethical triage, referral and continuity systems, and data-based advocacy rather than relying on individual sessions alone.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A limited grant can fund only one of several proposed supports. Which allocation process is most defensible?
choices: Award the grant to the department that submits the strongest and most persistent advocacy emails.
Split the small grant evenly across every proposed activity even where need and access differ sharply.
Weigh disaggregated need, expected benefit, access barriers, evidence, feasibility, and input, then monitor.
Choose the newest commercial program on the market so students benefit from current instructional design.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Equitable allocation is transparent and need responsive, considers barriers and likely effects, and monitors reach and outcomes rather than confusing equality with equity.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A dashboard will show counseling outcomes to staff. Which design best protects students?
choices: Display student names beside outcome counts so teachers can verify totals for their own homerooms.
Assume stripping student names from the table protects privacy even when subgroups contain two students.
Attach brief individual counseling notes to dashboard rows so staff understand why specific numbers shifted.
Report aggregate or suppressed data, restrict access, minimize fields, and block small-cell disclosure.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Program reporting should communicate useful evidence while applying privacy, data minimization, secure access, suppression, and current legal and district rules.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: What should a program communication plan include?
choices: Provide recurring accessible multilingual info on services, access, privacy limits, urgent help, and input.
Post one detailed technical handbook on the district website in August and refer families there all year.
Highlight promised improvement rates in flyers so more families feel confident referring their children.
Include real confidential student stories with minor name changes so community readers grasp counseling work.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Transparent, accessible communication clarifies program scope and access while protecting privacy and avoiding promises beyond the counselor’s role.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

chapterTakeaways: Triage daily demands transparently: handle imminent safety crises first, protect scheduled direct student services next, and guard preventive Tier 1 calendars against administrative drift.
Deliver virtual counseling and store records within FERPA-compliant platforms, confirming informed consent, private physical settings, and local emergency contacts before remote sessions.
Allocate counseling resources by disaggregated student need rather than uniform volume, share multilingual access pathways with families, and align professional learning to student gaps.

chapters.title: Program Assessment and Implementation Quality
chapters.summary: Use program and competency assessments, aligned evaluation designs, baseline and implementation evidence, and student voice to determine what is in place and what to improve.
objectives: Distinguish implementation assessment from outcome evaluation.
Use baseline, aligned measures, and fidelity data.
Convert assessment findings into prioritized improvement actions.
chapters.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

sections.heading: Program assessment asks what is in place
sections.content: A program assessment compares current components and practices with an articulated model or standard. It identifies strengths, partial implementation, gaps, and priorities for development. The process should use evidence rather than aspiration and involve the team responsible for improvement. A checklist result does not establish that student outcomes changed; it tells the program whether the structures and practices expected to support those outcomes are present and implemented.
sections.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

sections.heading: Competency assessment supports growth
sections.content: A professional standards and competencies assessment helps a counselor reflect on current knowledge, skills, mindsets, evidence, and development needs. Pair ratings with examples, supervision, performance feedback, student and program evidence, and a manageable learning goal. Revisit progress after supported practice. It is not an official test score, a diagnosis, or a substitute for state credentialing and district evaluation procedures.
sections.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

sections.heading: Aligned evaluation starts before delivery
sections.content: Define the student target and meaningful outcome, identify the population, record a comparable baseline, select measures aligned to the construct, establish data protections, and state a decision rule. Add pre/post or repeated learning checks, outcome indicators, participation, disaggregation, and qualitative feedback as appropriate. A measure chosen only because it is convenient or standardized may still be invalid for the decision the program needs to make.
sections.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

expandableCase.label: Applied practice case
expandableCase.title: Pre-Delivery Baseline and Aligned Evaluation for Senior FAFSA Lessons
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: Before delivering a six-week Grade 12 FAFSA and postsecondary planning classroom curriculum, a counselor plans to evaluate effectiveness solely through a five-point final-day survey asking seniors whether they enjoyed the slides and found the counselor approachable.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Establish pre-delivery FAFSA completion and knowledge baselines, align Mindsets & Behaviors and outcome measures, and set decision rules for targeted follow-up.
expandableCase.explanation: Satisfaction surveys capture perception rather than student learning or postsecondary behavior change. ASCA Assess standards require designing aligned evaluation before delivery—pairing participation, pre/post Mindset & Behaviors checks, and FAFSA completion rates with clear triggers for follow-up support.

sections.heading: Implementation evidence explains results
sections.content: Fidelity includes adherence to core components, dosage, quality, reach, participant responsiveness, and contextual adaptations. Weak outcomes with weak implementation do not fairly test the planned intervention. Strong implementation with weak outcomes suggests a poor fit, weak theory, insufficient intensity, or an inaccurate need definition. Strong outcomes with uneven reach require access improvement. Document adaptations so the team can learn which version produced which result.
sections.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Why should a counseling team complete a program assessment?
choices: Replace annual student outcome evaluation with a self-scored checklist of completed program components.
Compare current delivery with program standards, spot strengths and gaps, and set improvement priorities.
Convert every counseling workshop and check-in into an official numerical effectiveness score for the year.
Evaluate individual students’ diagnostic profiles to confirm whether outside clinical labels are accurate.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Program assessment examines implementation and alignment. It supports improvement but does not by itself establish student outcomes.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: What is the purpose of a professional standards and competencies assessment?
choices: Rank individual students on the caseload by urgency so counselors know who needs immediate intervention.
Generate an official ETS scaled readiness score showing whether a counselor meets state licensure cutoffs.
Identify practice strengths and growth areas, guide learning and supervision goals, and track reflection.
Replace state credential renewal rules and annual building administrator evaluations with self-assessment.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: A competency self-assessment supports reflective professional development; results require honest evidence, context, goals, and follow-up rather than punitive overinterpretation.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A team evaluates a new ninth-grade transition program. Why collect baseline data?
choices: A national percentile rank showing how each participating student compares with peers in other states.
Direct proof that any subsequent gain in student outcomes was caused solely by the counseling program.
A reliable substitute for tracking whether planned intervention sessions were actually delivered faithfully.
A defined starting benchmark against which later changes in target outcomes can be compared.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Baseline data establish the initial condition and help set targets and interpret trends; causal conclusions still require appropriate design and consideration of alternatives.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A lesson series shows no outcome improvement, but half the planned sessions were canceled. What should the team conclude?
choices: Delivery was too incomplete to judge the plan fairly; fix implementation and collect fresh outcome data.
The underlying intervention theory is shown to be ineffective for this school and should be retired.
Students in the grade level lacked willingness to engage with the lessons and apply the skills taught.
Implementation fidelity does not alter conclusions once pre- and post-outcome numbers are available.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Outcome interpretation must include adherence, dosage, quality, participation, and contextual disruptions. Weak implementation and weak theory require different responses.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Which evaluation plan best assesses a classroom lesson series?
choices: Use an unrelated statewide math test score because standardized scores appear more objective to leaders.
Define the target, pair aligned pre/post measures with fidelity and reach data, disaggregate, and ask students.
Count how many slide decks and handouts were completed and infer that students mastered the objectives.
Interview one enthusiastic student after the final class to confirm whether the lesson series succeeded.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: A coherent evaluation aligns measures with the goal and includes implementation, learning, outcomes, equity, and stakeholder experience.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

chapterTakeaways: Separate program assessment from student outcome evaluation: the ASCA School Counseling Program Assessment checks which structural components are in place, whereas results reports judge student impact.
Use the ASCA School Counselor Professional Standards and Competencies self-assessment to identify individual growth priorities, supervision needs, and targeted continuing education goals.
Design evaluation before delivering an intervention by collecting aligned baseline or pre-test data and tracking implementation fidelity so post-test changes can be interpreted accurately.

chapters.title: Results Data, Interpretation, and Reporting
chapters.summary: Interpret aggregate and disaggregated results cautiously, triangulate mixed evidence, avoid unsupported causal claims, and report actionable findings without compromising privacy.
objectives: Disaggregate outcomes and examine access.
Interpret surveys, comparisons, and mixed evidence cautiously.
Build plain-language results reports with limitations and next actions.
chapters.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

sections.heading: Disaggregation reveals who benefits
sections.content: A favorable schoolwide average can coexist with a worsening gap. Break down achievement, attendance, behavior, participation, and learning data by relevant grade, program, and student groups when lawful and statistically responsible. Check denominator size, missingness, opportunity, and small-cell privacy. Describe patterns without blaming groups, combine them with student and family evidence, and examine policies or access conditions that could explain unequal reach or outcomes.
sections.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

sections.heading: Survey and qualitative evidence
sections.content: Write neutral, clear, single-focus items with response options that fit the question and intended audience. Pilot wording and accessibility, offer needed language and communication access, and examine who did not respond. Interviews and focus groups add meaning but require consent, privacy, skilled facilitation, and transparent selection. Treat stakeholder voice as evidence, not decoration, and distinguish common themes from isolated but potentially important experiences.
sections.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

sections.heading: Association is not automatically causation
sections.content: Students who choose a service may differ from students who do not. Maturation, concurrent initiatives, historical events, regression, and measurement change can also explain improvement. Acknowledge design limits and say the program contributed to or was associated with change unless stronger methods support causal inference. Baseline, repeated measures, credible comparisons, fidelity, and converging evidence strengthen conclusions but do not erase every alternative explanation.
sections.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

sections.heading: A useful results report leads to a decision
sections.content: State the need and goal, intended population, services, reach and dosage, learning evidence, outcome evidence, disaggregated patterns, implementation, stakeholder voice, limitations, and the next action and review date. Use plain language, labeled visuals, definitions, and context. Protect confidentiality through aggregation, suppression, and access controls. Report unfavorable results as honestly as favorable ones and distinguish findings from recommendations.
sections.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

expandableCase.label: Applied practice case
expandableCase.title: Transparent Disaggregated Results Reporting for a Grade 6 Attendance Group
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A Grade 6 attendance group (n=14) increased mean attendance from 83% to 91%, yet three students facing morning bus barriers showed zero gain and two sessions were canceled for state testing. A draft faculty slide claims the group "proved 100% effectiveness" across campus.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Report disaggregated results with clear visuals, dosage limitations, and transportation follow-up rather than claiming universal causal proof.
expandableCase.explanation: Decision-focused ASCA results reports connect participation, learning, and outcome evidence to next-step improvements. Disclosing small sample size, missed sessions, and non-responder needs avoids misleading causal claims while directing team advocacy toward concrete transportation barriers.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A program’s overall attendance improved, but one student group’s gap widened. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Conclude that the subgroup caused its own widening gap and add individual accountability contracts.
Omit subgroup disaggregation from stakeholder reports because discussing disparities can feel uncomfortable.
Report both the schoolwide gain and the growing subgroup disparity, study barriers, and refine services.
Highlight the favorable schoolwide trend in the report while saving subgroup disaggregation tables for later.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Aggregate results can conceal inequitable outcomes. Ethical evaluation disaggregates responsibly and uses the pattern to examine systems and target improvement.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A results report says a group “caused” higher graduation rates because participants improved. What is the main problem?
choices: Strong group participation counts establish direct causation whenever participants graduate at higher rates.
Causation can be claimed only when every participant in the group achieves the exact same grade-point gain.
School-level graduation records are too subjective to cite in a public results summary for stakeholders.
Without controlling selection and outside factors, data support association or contribution, not causation.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Pre/post or comparison patterns can be useful, but selection, maturation, other supports, and context limit causal inference unless the design addresses them.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A needs survey asks, “How helpful was our excellent counseling program?” What is the main concern?
choices: The leading phrasing biases responses upward; revise into neutral, clear items and pilot with users.
Item phrasing rarely influences survey results as long as students submit their ratings anonymously.
The survey item is problematic only if the rating scale offers fewer than five numbered response choices.
Positive wording encourages honest engagement and helps respondents recall helpful counseling moments.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Neutral wording, accessible language, appropriate response options, piloting, and attention to nonresponse improve the usefulness of survey evidence.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Which results-report format best supports stakeholder understanding?
choices: Display dense statistical tables without plain-language definitions so the report looks rigorously technical.
Share goal, services, reach, learning and outcome data, gaps, limits, student voice, actions, and privacy.
Attach raw identifiable student spreadsheets to the report so families and leaders can inspect every case.
Present a detailed count of meetings and lessons completed while leaving student outcomes out for brevity.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: A clear results report connects purpose, implementation, evidence, limitations, equity, and decisions while protecting confidentiality.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Three data sources point in different directions about school belonging. What should the counselor do?
choices: Average the three different belonging indicators together into one composite number to resolve conflict.
Report that belonging improved because at least one of the three sources moved in a positive direction.
Check measure quality, groups, timing, delivery, and context, and gather more evidence instead of forcing fit.
Drop the two smaller data sources and base every program decision on whichever dataset had the most replies.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Triangulation is not automatic agreement. Divergence can reveal subgroup differences, measurement limitations, timing effects, or new questions requiring follow-up.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

chapterTakeaways: Always disaggregate schoolwide results by race, ethnicity, gender, socioeconomic status, language, and disability to expose hidden opportunity gaps that aggregate averages conceal.
Interpret program results with scientific humility: pre-post gains and correlations show association rather than definitive causation when comparison groups or external confounders are uncontrolled.
Pair quantitative participation and outcome metrics with qualitative student and family voice in concise plain-language results reports that state limitations and recommend specific next actions.

chapters.title: Continuous Improvement and Data-Based Advocacy
chapters.summary: Turn evaluation into transparent choices about what to retain, adapt, stop, scale, resource, and monitor while keeping equity and stakeholder learning central.
objectives: Use decision rules and stakeholder feedback to revise programs.
Communicate misses and limitations honestly.
Build evidence-based advocacy and responsible scaling plans.
chapters.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

sections.heading: Improvement is a disciplined learning cycle
sections.content: Compare actual implementation and outcomes with the goal and prespecified decision rule. Ask which students participated, learned, and improved; which did not; what barriers and adaptations occurred; and what the data cannot establish. Retain effective components, address access and fidelity problems, change weak strategies, and identify one testable next step. Specify the responsible person, resources, timeline, and next review so reflection becomes implementation.
sections.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

sections.heading: Transparent communication builds credibility
sections.content: If a goal is missed, report the result, data quality, implementation, context, and limitations without changing the goal after seeing results or blaming students and families. Explain what was learned and the evidence-informed revision. If a goal is met, avoid overclaiming causality or permanence. Give stakeholders accessible opportunities to question interpretations and contribute contextual knowledge before final decisions are made.
sections.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

sections.heading: Data-based advocacy connects need to a feasible ask
sections.content: An advocacy case combines disaggregated local need, student and family voice, service access, counselor time and capacity, credible research, applicable standards, and a specific resource or policy request. Describe how the proposal would work, likely barriers, costs, alternatives, and how impact will be evaluated. Protect confidentiality and avoid relying only on emotionally vivid cases or a national benchmark detached from local conditions.
sections.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

sections.heading: Scale only after checking durability and fit
sections.content: A promising intervention should show adequate implementation, meaningful outcomes, acceptable burden, equitable reach, and stakeholder support. Before expansion, identify core components versus adaptable features, resource and training needs, data protections, and likely contextual differences. Pilot responsibly, monitor unintended effects, and build feedback loops. Sustainability depends on ownership, routines, staffing, funding, leadership, and evidence that continues after initial enthusiasm.
sections.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

expandableCase.label: Applied practice case
expandableCase.title: Phased Scaling of a Grant-Funded Grade 9 Peer-Mentoring Pilot
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A pilot Grade 9 peer-mentoring transition program in one academy cut first-semester course failures by 22% using two grant-funded coordinator stipends and weekly counselor coaching. District leaders propose mandating immediate unfunded expansion to all six high schools next month.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Identify core components, evaluate fidelity, staffing capacity, and equitable reach, and propose a phased, sustainably funded scale-up plan.
expandableCase.explanation: Expanding an intervention rapidly without protecting core components such as mentor training, coaching, and time undermines fidelity and widens site inequities. ASCA continuous-improvement advocacy pairs durability evidence with realistic resourcing and ongoing monitoring before districtwide mandates.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A targeted intervention met its average outcome goal but not for students who missed sessions because of transportation barriers. What is the best next step?
choices: Declare the targeted initiative a complete success because the group met its average outcome benchmark.
Lower the outcome target for students facing transit barriers so their final numbers meet the goal.
Cancel the intervention for every student next term because it did not work equally for all participants.
Keep effective elements, remove the transit barrier, adapt delivery, and monitor affected students’ gains.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Continuous improvement distinguishes effectiveness from reach and equity, preserves helpful elements, removes access barriers, and tests adaptations with data.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A program result is weaker than expected. How should the counselor communicate it?
choices: Report the shortfall and limits honestly, explain lessons learned, and share a specific revision plan.
Substitute a different indicator that improved after seeing results and present it as the original target.
Explain that student and family follow-through caused the gap while keeping the current plan unchanged.
Withhold the weaker outcome from the annual report so stakeholders maintain confidence in the program.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Transparent reporting builds trust and learning. A missed goal can guide improvement when evidence, limitations, and next decisions are communicated without blame.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Which evidence makes the strongest case for adding another counselor position?
choices: A brief written statement explaining that current counselors feel stretched thin during busy months.
Local needs, access and time-use data, gaps, capacity, research, a staffing plan, and impact metrics.
Confidential student stories with recognizable details illustrating how severe individual crises have become.
A national counselor-to-student ratio guideline quoted alone without local caseload or outcome context.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Data-based advocacy integrates local need, capacity, equity, research, feasible resources, privacy, and an evaluation plan.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A closing-the-gap initiative reduces a course-access disparity. What should happen next?
choices: Revert to the previous enrollment procedure right away now that this year’s disparity numbers improved.
Mandate the initiative across every district school immediately before checking local implementation quality.
Monitor durability and unintended effects, collect stakeholder feedback, refine steps, and scale thoughtfully.
Move focus elsewhere and assume the narrowed course-access gap will stay closed without routine checks.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Improvement requires follow-up for maintenance, equity, implementation, and unintended consequences before scaling.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: How should a counselor choose the next program priority after annual evaluation?
choices: Choose the simplest activity to run next year so the team can post quick early wins regardless of need.
Select whichever topic aligns most closely with the counselor’s favorite workshop materials and interests.
Pick the issue with the largest raw incident count without examining subgroup rates, severity, or impact.
Integrate outcome gaps, student and family voice, urgency, safety, equity, feasibility, evidence, and mission.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Program priorities require transparent judgment across need, voice, risk, equity, feasibility, evidence, alignment, and available capacity.
knowledgeChecks.reviewNote: Independently authored and source reviewed for study use; independent school-counselor validation remains pending.

chapterTakeaways: Use transparent decision rules after reviewing results reports to decide what to retain, revise, discontinue, or scale, treating unmet targets as diagnostic feedback rather than hiding misses.
Frame data-based systemic advocacy around disaggregated student equity gaps paired with a concrete, feasible policy or resource ask aligned to district priorities.
Pilot and evaluate fidelity, equity impact, and contextual fit before scaling a counseling intervention schoolwide so local success translates durably across classrooms.

diagrams.title: Direct vs. Indirect Student Services and Counselor Role Boundaries
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Differentiate appropriate direct and indirect student services from inappropriate non-counseling duties when prioritizing counselor time and advocating with administrators.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow clarifying how counselor time balances direct student services, indirect student supports, and data-backed role advocacy.

accessibility.shortAlt: Role boundary flow distinguishing direct student services and indirect supports from non-counseling duties via advocacy.
accessibility.longDescription: Read left to right. Counselors align at least 80 percent of time to direct services (instruction, appraisal and advisement, short-term counseling) and indirect services (consultation, collaboration, referrals). Distinguishing these core duties from inappropriate clerical or disciplinary tasks equips counselors for data-based role advocacy with administrators.
textEquivalent: Use-of-time alignment prioritizes at least 80 percent of school counselor time for direct and indirect services directly benefiting students.
Direct student services involve face-to-face delivery through school counseling instruction, individual or small-group appraisal and advisement, and short-term counseling.
Indirect student services occur on behalf of students via parent and teacher consultation, multidisciplinary collaboration, and community referrals.
Inappropriate duties such as routine discipline enforcement, master scheduling clerking, or primary testing coordination undermine student access and counselor neutrality.
Data-based role advocacy uses time-use logs and student outcome evidence in the annual administrative conference to reassign non-counseling tasks.

nodes.label: 1. Student-centered time alignment
nodes.detail: Structure weekly schedules so roughly 80 percent or more of counselor time delivers direct and indirect student services rather than building operations.

nodes.label: 2. Direct services with students
nodes.detail: Deliver proactive classroom lessons, individualized academic and career appraisal and advisement, and brief solution-focused or skill-building counseling.

nodes.label: 3. Indirect services on students’ behalf
nodes.detail: Consult with families and teachers, collaborate on MTSS, IEP, and 504 teams, and connect students to vetted community clinical or basic-needs providers.

nodes.label: 4. Non-counseling duty boundary
nodes.detail: Identify tasks that conflict with counseling ethics or access, including administering discipline, supervising lunch duty, primary test coordination, or clerical data entry.

nodes.label: 5. Data-backed role advocacy
nodes.detail: Present time-use audits and student outcome gains during the annual administrative conference to negotiate realistic reassignment of non-counseling duties.

edges.label: anchors face-to-face student delivery
pairs with systemic team and family support
contrasts core roles against clerical duties
triggers evidence-based role realignment

diagrams.title: Developmental, Learning, and Ecological Lenses for Student Support Design
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Synthesize psychosocial stages, cognitive scaffolding, learning mechanisms, and family-ecological context as flexible lenses for designing developmentally responsive counseling supports.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow showing how psychosocial, cognitive, learning, and ecological frameworks converge into flexible student counseling supports.

accessibility.shortAlt: Concept flow combining psychosocial stages, cognitive scaffolding, learning theories, and ecological systems into flexible counseling support design.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. School counselors integrate four complementary lenses rather than treating any single theory as a rigid label. Psychosocial theory highlights mastery and identity tasks across elementary through high school. Cognitive and sociocultural frameworks guide concrete-to-abstract scaffolding within the zone of proximal development. Behavioral, cognitive, and social learning explain reinforcement, appraisal, and modeling. Family and ecological systems anchor cultural responsiveness so supports fit the whole student context.
textEquivalent: Examine Erikson psychosocial tasks such as industry versus inferiority and identity versus role confusion to align counseling with competence and belonging needs.
Match task abstraction to concrete or formal operational reasoning while using Vygotsky zone-of-proximal-development scaffolding.
Apply behavioral reinforcement, cognitive appraisal reframing, and social-learning modeling to build self-efficacy and coping skills.
Situate student behavior within family systems, peer norms, school climate, and cultural strengths rather than isolating the child.
Synthesize all four lenses into flexible, strengths-based classroom, group, or individual supports without using developmental stages as rigid labels.

nodes.label: 1. Psychosocial stage tasks (Erikson)
nodes.detail: Consider developmental needs for competence during industry versus inferiority in elementary years and coherent belonging during identity versus role confusion in adolescence.

nodes.label: 2. Cognitive readiness and ZPD scaffolding
nodes.detail: Adjust counseling language and visuals for concrete versus formal operational thinking while providing structured zone-of-proximal-development scaffolds.

nodes.label: 3. Behavioral, cognitive, and social learning
nodes.detail: Combine positive reinforcement, cognitive appraisal checks, and peer or adult modeling to strengthen adaptive habits and self-efficacy.

nodes.label: 4. Family systems and ecological context
nodes.detail: Interpret student patterns through interconnected family roles, cultural values, school climate, and systemic opportunities rather than deficit assumptions.

nodes.label: 5. Flexible, non-labeling support design
nodes.detail: Translate developmental and ecological insights into developmentally appropriate lessons, advisement, and brief interventions without treating theories as diagnoses.

edges.label: pairs identity needs with reasoning level
guides how new skills are modeled and practiced
grounds skill transfer in family and culture
shapes responsive, strengths-based services

diagrams.title: Confidentiality, Informed Consent, and Duty-to-Warn / Reporting Flow
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Apply ASCA ethical standards and statutory duties when explaining confidentiality limits, assessing imminent harm or abuse, and executing protective reporting.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow tracing upfront confidentiality disclosure, imminent-risk or abuse triage, statutory reporting and warm handoff, and objective documentation.

accessibility.shortAlt: Ethical decision flow from upfront confidentiality limits through harm or abuse evaluation to statutory reporting and documentation.
accessibility.longDescription: Read left to right. Counselors explain confidentiality and its safety limits upfront without promising secrecy. When risk arises, they evaluate imminent harm to self or others or suspected abuse/neglect, then activate statutory reporting, supervision, and warm handoffs. Sharing stays limited to safety-essential facts, followed by objective FERPA-compliant documentation.
textEquivalent: Explain confidentiality and its legal and ethical limits upfront in student-friendly language, never promising secrecy about danger or abuse.

memoryAids.title: Role Lens: Lead, Advocate, Collaborate, Consult, Manage
memoryAids.content: When choices all sound helpful, ask which professional role is needed and whether the response preserves shared ownership, student access, ethical boundaries, and program outcomes.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Three Student Domains: A-C-S/E
memoryAids.content: Track the complete program through Academic, Career, and Social/Emotional development. A choice that collapses counseling into only one domain is usually incomplete.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Development Is a Lens, Not a Label
memoryAids.content: Use stage and learning theories to predict supports and questions, then verify with the individual student and context. Age or theory alone never becomes a diagnosis.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Privacy: Explain, Protect, Limit, Document
memoryAids.content: Explain privacy and foreseeable limits early, protect information, disclose only when authorized or required and only as needed, then document the basis and follow-up.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Safety Overrides Secrecy Promises
memoryAids.content: For imminent danger, maintain supervision and activate current crisis procedures. For suspected abuse, follow the jurisdiction’s mandated-reporting process without investigating independently.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Ethical STEPS: Standards, Team, Effects, Protect, Study
memoryAids.content: Review standards and law, consult an appropriate team, compare likely effects and power dynamics, protect student rights and safety, then study the outcome and revise.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Brief Counseling: Connect, Clarify, Choose, Check
memoryAids.content: Build the relationship, clarify need and safety, choose a theory-linked student action, and check progress. Refer with continuity when the need exceeds school scope or competence.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Service Match: All, Some, Few
memoryAids.content: Use classroom or schoolwide services for common needs, targeted groups for shared needs, and individual or intensive supports for fewer students based on evidence and safety.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Group Safety Before Cohesion
memoryAids.content: Screen for fit and risk, explain purpose and privacy limits, teach norms, build low-risk participation, and refer students whose needs exceed the group’s purpose or safety.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Bullying Is Not Balanced Conflict
memoryAids.content: Mediation requires safe voluntary participation and relative power balance. Bullying calls for protection, policy-based response, accountability, and attention to the power difference.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Consultation: Define, Plan, Do, Review
memoryAids.content: Operationalize the concern, define a shared goal and roles, implement a feasible strategy, then review fidelity, outcomes, feasibility, and student or family experience.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: MTSS: Intensity, Not Identity
memoryAids.content: A tier names support intensity, not the kind of student. Maintain universal supports, add targeted or intensive help based on response data, and never use MTSS to delay required evaluation.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Referral: Match, Consent, Access, Connect, Follow
memoryAids.content: Match the resource to need, obtain required consent for coordination, address access barriers, confirm connection, follow up, and continue appropriate school-based support.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Vision Is Future; Mission Is Present Purpose
memoryAids.content: Vision states the desired equitable future for students. Mission states whom the program serves, what it does now, across which domains, and how it supports the school mission.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Data Story: Participate, Learn, Improve
memoryAids.content: Participation shows who received what; learning shows targeted knowledge, attitude, or skill; outcomes show achievement, attendance, or behavior change. Strong reports connect all three.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Goal Formula: Group + Baseline + Outcome + Target + Time
memoryAids.content: A measurable annual student outcome goal names the population, documented starting point, meaningful outcome, realistic magnitude or criterion, deadline, and equity context.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Measurement: Consistent Is Not Necessarily Valid
memoryAids.content: Reliability is consistency or precision. Validity is support for a specific interpretation and use. A measure can score consistently while being used for the wrong construct or decision.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Evaluation: Baseline, Delivery, Learning, Outcome, Equity
memoryAids.content: Define the starting point, verify what was delivered and to whom, measure target learning and meaningful outcomes, disaggregate results, and include limitations before deciding.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Report Both the Average and the Gap
memoryAids.content: A schoolwide gain can hide worsening access or outcomes for a group. Report aggregate and responsible disaggregated results, protect small cells, investigate barriers, and adjust.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

memoryAids.title: Improve: Retain, Repair, Replace, Review
memoryAids.content: Retain effective core components, repair access or fidelity barriers, replace weak strategies when evidence warrants, and set a dated review with defined implementation and outcome data.
memoryAids.reviewNote: Retrieval cue only; apply the underlying concept and verify current law, ethics, standards, and district requirements.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: ASCA ethical confidentiality and duty-to-warn analysis
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Balance Student Privacy, Mandated Reporting, and Parent Notification
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Apply the ASCA Ethical Standards for School Counselors, mandated-reporting duties, and FERPA need-to-know boundaries when a student discloses physical abuse and nonsuicidal self-injury while an administrator demands session details.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Jordan (age 15, Grade 10) arrives shaken and asks for total secrecy before sharing that an older cousin at home struck them twice this week, bruising their shoulder, and that they cut their forearm last night to cope without suicidal intent. Five minutes later, an assistant principal texts asking why Jordan missed chemistry and requesting a summary of the disclosure. Intake forms previously explained confidentiality limits.
taskParts: Identify which elements of Jordan's disclosure legally and ethically require breaching confidentiality (suspected abuse and self-harm safety) and explain how to tell Jordan transparently.
Sequence immediate safety steps, including mandated child-protective reporting, nonsuicidal self-injury risk screening, and caregiver notification safeguards when household abuse is alleged.
Explain how to respond to the assistant principal's text message in alignment with ASCA confidentiality standards and FERPA legitimate educational interest.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Separate three distinct facts: physical injury by a household member (mandated report), forearm cutting without stated suicidal intent (still requires safety check), and an administrator's attendance inquiry.

planningFrame.label: Professional framework
planningFrame.guidance: Use ASCA Ethical Standards (A.2 confidentiality, A.9 serious and foreseeable harm, A.12 child abuse reporting), state mandated-reporter statutes, and FERPA need-to-know limits.

planningFrame.label: Action plan
planningFrame.guidance: Decline promising absolute secrecy, assess immediate medical and suicide risk, file a mandated CPS report promptly, involve Jordan in safety planning, and verify attendance only to the administrator.

planningFrame.label: Follow-up & ethics
planningFrame.guidance: Consult CPS/policy before contacting caregivers if doing so increases abuse risk, document objective facts in protected notes, and arrange ongoing check-ins and outside clinical referrals.

successCriteria: Refuses to promise unconditional secrecy and compassionately reminds Jordan of the foreseeable-harm and abuse-reporting limits reviewed at intake.
Immediately initiates a mandated child-abuse report without conducting an independent forensic investigation of the cousin.
Assesses both medical care for the forearm cut and potential suicide risk even though Jordan denies suicidal intent, coordinating safe caregiver notification per CPS guidance.
Limits communication with the assistant principal to attendance verification unless a specific school-safety need-to-know applies, avoiding casual text summaries.
commonPitfalls: Promising Jordan complete confidentiality to preserve rapport, then feeling trapped when mandated reporting is triggered.
Calling the household immediately to confront the family before checking whether notifying caregivers could endanger Jordan or compromise CPS.
Texting confidential abuse and self-harm details to the assistant principal over an unencrypted message because the administrator outranks the counselor.
Dismissing self-harm screening simply because Jordan stated they did not intend to die.
sampleOutline: Transparent boundaries: Acknowledge Jordan's courage, avoid promising secrecy, and clearly state the legal duty to keep them safe around physical abuse and self-injury.
Safety & reporting sequence: Check whether the bruise or forearm cut needs nurse attention, screen for covert suicidal ideation, and immediately file the mandated CPS report per statute.
Caregiver notification safeguard: Follow CPS and district protocol on notifying non-offending guardians so reporting does not escalate home danger.
FERPA & staff boundary: Reply briefly (not with sensitive details via text) confirming Jordan is excused in counseling, and document objective actions in secure, separate records.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: Disaggregated equity audit and closing-the-gap plan
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Design a Closing-the-Gap Plan From Disaggregated Ninth-Grade Failure Data
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Use ASCA National Model Manage tools—disaggregated school data, annual student outcome goals, closing-the-gap action plans, and use-of-time reallocation—to address hidden ninth-grade Algebra I inequities.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Schoolwide ninth-grade Algebra I pass rates sit at 82 percent, yet disaggregated data show only 54 percent of multilingual learners and 58 percent of low-income students passed, compared with 91 percent of higher-income English-proficient peers. Attendance records show 63 percent of failing students missed eight or more fall days, and counselor time logs show 44 percent of hours went to master-schedule clerical fixes and lunch duty.
taskParts: Interpret the disaggregated achievement, attendance, and counselor use-of-time data to pinpoint the core equity gap obscured by the 82 percent aggregate average.
Draft a measurable ASCA Annual Student Outcome Goal and aligned Closing-the-Gap Action Plan targeting both Algebra I credit attainment and chronic absenteeism.
Formulate a data-based administrative conference proposal to shift non-counseling clerical and lunch-duty hours toward the ASCA 80 percent direct/indirect student service benchmark.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Highlight the 33-to-37 percentage point pass-rate gaps for multilingual and low-income ninth graders, the 63% overlap with fall absences, and the 44% non-counseling time drain.

planningFrame.label: Professional framework
planningFrame.guidance: Apply the ASCA National Model Manage component: School Data Summary, Annual Student Outcome Goal, Closing-the-Gap Action Plan, Use-of-Time Calculator, and Annual Administrative Conference.

planningFrame.label: Action plan
planningFrame.guidance: Combine Tier 1 study/goal-setting lessons, Tier 2 attendance/credit-recovery small groups with bilingual family outreach, and math-department collaboration around tutoring access.

planningFrame.label: Follow-up & ethics
planningFrame.guidance: Track participation, Mindsets & Behaviors pre/post gains, and semester Algebra I pass and attendance outcomes while protecting individual student privacy in public equity reports.

successCriteria: Explains how the 82 percent building aggregate masks a 33-to-37 point equity gap affecting multilingual and economically disadvantaged ninth graders.
Links attendance patterns (63% missing eight or more days) to a concrete, measurable outcome goal with baseline, target, subgroup, and timeline.
Selects ASCA Mindsets & Behaviors standards paired with direct (classroom/group/individual) and indirect (family/teacher collaboration) interventions.
Uses the 44% non-counseling time audit constructively during an Annual Administrative Conference to advocate for the ASCA 80/20 direct-indirect service allocation.
commonPitfalls: Accepting the 82 percent schoolwide pass rate as acceptable and planning only generic schoolwide motivation assemblies.
Writing a Closing-the-Gap goal focused only on how many meetings counselors hold (participation data) rather than student pass rates and attendance (outcome data).
Confronting the principal about lunch duty without connecting reclaimed counselor hours directly to ninth-grade credit recovery and graduation outcomes.
Blaming student motivation while ignoring language access, transportation/attendance barriers, and classroom instructional supports.
sampleOutline: Equity diagnosis: Aggregate 82% pass rate hides 33-to-37 point gaps for multilingual (54%) and low-income (58%) freshmen, heavily compounded by chronic fall absences (63%).

Outcome goal & action plan: Target raising multilingual and low-income Algebra I pass rates by 15 percentage points and cutting absences below 5 days via targeted check-ins, tutoring links, and bilingual family nights.
Use-of-time advocacy: Present the 44% clerical/lunch-duty log at the Annual Administrative Conference to reassign fair-share non-counseling duties and reach the 80% student-service standard.
Assessment & reporting: Collect pre/post Mindsets & Behaviors data alongside quarter grades and attendance, sharing disaggregated progress with the advisory council.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Pair Universal Coping Lessons With Targeted Attendance Small-Group Support
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Design a tiered Deliver plan combining Tier 1 school counseling classroom instruction with ethically screened Tier 2 small-group counseling while resolving teacher scheduling and parent-consent requests.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Fall screening of 420 sixth graders shows 68 percent report moderate test worry and weak planner habits during the middle-school transition, while 14 students already have 5 to 7 unexcused absences and frequent morning nurse visits. Teachers ask you to pull all 14 students into one large coping group during core math class without parent permission slips, arguing that counseling is standard general-education programming.
taskParts: Justify why the 68 percent universal transition need belongs in Tier 1 classroom lessons while the 14 chronically absent students require Tier 2 small-group intervention.
Correct the teachers' group-design request regarding optimal group size, screening/composition, rotating schedules to protect core math instruction, and written parental consent.
Outline group confidentiality limits, developmental norms for sixth graders, and pre/post metrics linking sessions to morning attendance and nurse-visit reductions.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Distinguish the broad Tier 1 signal (68% of 420 sixth graders with test worry/organization needs) from the high-need Tier 2 cluster (14 students with 5 to 7 absences and somatic nurse visits).

planningFrame.label: Professional framework
planningFrame.guidance: Apply ASCA Deliver tiered services (classroom instruction vs. small-group counseling), ASCA Ethical Standard A.7 (group work), and MTSS alignment.

planningFrame.label: Action plan
planningFrame.guidance: Deliver 3 universal sixth-grade executive-functioning and coping lessons, split the 14 students after individual screening into two 6-to-7-student groups on a rotating non-math schedule, and secure caregiver consent.

planningFrame.label: Follow-up & ethics
planningFrame.guidance: Explain that group confidentiality is encouraged but cannot be guaranteed among peers, coordinate with the school nurse on somatic triggers, and monitor weekly attendance.

successCriteria: Matches Tier 1 classroom instruction to the 68 percent universal transition need and Tier 2 small-group counseling to the 14 high-absence students.
Splits the 14 students into smaller developmentally appropriate groups (typically 5 to 8 middle schoolers) following brief individual screening rather than forming one 14-student group.
Protects core math access via rotating or non-core scheduling and secures active written parental/guardian permission before small-group participation.
Addresses group-confidentiality limits explicitly and links nurse collaboration plus attendance logs to pre/post evaluation.
commonPitfalls: Placing all 14 sixth graders into a single group, which weakens psychological safety, peer participation, and counseling effectiveness.
Pulling struggling students repeatedly from the same core math block, inadvertently compounding academic anxiety and avoidance.
Skipping written parent/guardian consent for small-group counseling by treating targeted group sessions as identical to universal classroom lessons.
Promising sixth graders absolute peer confidentiality inside a group rather than teaching norms while acknowledging limits.
sampleOutline: Tiered match: Serve the 68% transition need through Tier 1 classroom lessons on planner routines and test-anxiety strategies; reserve Tier 2 groups for the 14 students with absences and nurse visits.
Ethical group structure: Screen each of the 14 students individually, obtain written parent/guardian permission, form two balanced groups of 6 to 7, and rotate meeting times outside core math.
Group norms & collaboration: Teach realistic peer-confidentiality boundaries, align coping plans with the school nurse, and involve caregivers in morning routines.
Progress tracking: Measure Mindsets & Behaviors pre/post coping mastery alongside six-week reductions in unexcused absences and morning nurse visits.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: Suicide-risk triage, parent notification, and referral protocol
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Execute Imminent Suicide-Risk Triage and Warm Handoff After a Peer Report
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Sequence immediate suicide-risk screening, continuous supervision, parent notification, crisis referral, and school re-entry planning for an eleventh grader with active ideation and access to lethal means.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: At 1:45 PM, two juniors show you a screenshot where friend Maya wrote "I cannot do this anymore and everyone is better off without me" after a breakup and cyberbullying. Privately, Maya admits wishing she would not wake up, knows where her stepfather keeps sleeping pills, and begs you not to call her mother because she gets angry under stress. Bus dismissal is in 45 minutes, and Maya has a Section 504 plan for anxiety.
taskParts: Identify Maya's acute suicide risk indicators (ideation, hopelessness, access to sleeping pills, recent stressors, and impending 45-minute dismissal) and specify non-negotiable immediate supervision rules.
Outline how to conduct a structured risk screening, notify Maya's mother ethically despite Maya's plea, and arrange a warm handoff to emergency or clinical crisis services.
Plan the post-crisis re-entry meeting, cyberbullying safety follow-up, and review of Maya's existing Section 504 anxiety accommodations upon her return.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Flag high-imminence risk markers: explicit hopelessness message, passive-to-active ideation, identified access to sleeping pills, acute cyberbullying trigger, and bus dismissal in 45 minutes.

planningFrame.label: Professional framework
planningFrame.guidance: Apply ASCA Ethical Standard A.9 (serious and foreseeable harm), structured school suicide-risk protocol, lethal-means counseling for guardians, and Section 504 review duties.

planningFrame.label: Action plan
planningFrame.guidance: Keep Maya under continuous adult supervision (never send her to the bus alone), notify her mother directly with calm collaboration and lethal-means safety steps, and facilitate same-day crisis evaluation.

planningFrame.label: Follow-up & ethics
planningFrame.guidance: Thank and check in with the reporting peers without disclosing Maya's session details, document notifications objectively, and hold a re-entry and 504-review meeting before return.

successCriteria: Maintains continuous, unbroken adult supervision from 1:45 PM until Maya is safely transferred to her guardian or emergency crisis responders—never releasing her to the school bus.
Notifies Maya's mother despite her request for secrecy under ASCA A.9 while involving Maya in how the call is framed and advising safe locking of the sleeping pills.
Completes district suicide-risk documentation, initiates a warm referral to qualified crisis/clinical evaluators, and avoids relying on a discredited no-suicide contract.
Plans structured school re-entry, cyberbullying administrative intervention, peer-reporter check-in, and a Section 504 team review of Maya's anxiety supports.
commonPitfalls: Honoring Maya's plea not to call her mother to protect counseling rapport when imminent lethal-means risk is present.
Having Maya sign a written "no-harm contract" and allowing her to ride the 2:30 PM bus home alone.
Attempting to provide long-term clinical suicide therapy inside the school counseling office instead of facilitating immediate outside clinical crisis evaluation.
Revealing Maya's risk-assessment details back to the two friends who reported the screenshot.
sampleOutline: Immediate safety & supervision: Keep Maya with a trusted adult at all times; suspend routine bus dismissal and run the district's structured suicide-risk screener.

Guardian notification & means safety: Transparently inform Maya that safety requires calling her mother; invite Maya's input, brief her mother calmly on immediate crisis evaluation, and emphasize securing sleeping pills.
Warm referral & documentation: Coordinate same-day crisis assessment (or emergency transport if guardian cannot safely assume care) and log objective risk actions per district policy.
Re-entry & 504 alignment: Check in confidentially with reporting peers, address cyberbullying through school policy, and convene a re-entry and Section 504 review meeting prior to Maya's return.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: ASCA Assess program evaluation and results reporting
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Separate Participation, Mindsets and Behaviors, and Outcome Evidence
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Evaluate mixed small-group results data using the ASCA Assess framework, resist an unsupported building-wide causal claim, and design an ethical, improvement-focused results report.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: After a six-week eighth-grade conflict group for 10 students with fighting referrals, surveys show 9 of 10 enjoyed the group and 8 of 10 named three de-escalation steps on a vignette. Discipline logs show referrals fell for 4 students, stayed flat for 4, and rose for 2 who missed half the sessions from bus tardiness. The principal asks for a one-page brief proving your group caused the school's 12 percent overall referral drop.
taskParts: Classify every metric in the scenario into ASCA participation, Mindsets & Behaviors (learning/perception), and outcome data, explaining why enjoyment alone cannot verify behavior transfer.
Explain methodologically why the small group cannot be credited as the cause of the building's 12 percent overall referral decline and how to respond transparently to the principal.
Propose concrete program revisions informed by the flat-response subgroup (4 students) and the bus-tardiness dosage barrier (2 students).

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Distinguish participation (10 enrolled, 2 missed half the sessions), Mindsets & Behaviors (8 of 10 named steps; 9 of 10 liked it), and outcome results (4 improved, 4 flat, 2 increased).

planningFrame.label: Professional framework
planningFrame.guidance: Apply ASCA National Model Assess standards (Small-Group Results Report), evidence triangulation, implementation-dosage analysis, and honest limits on causal inference.

planningFrame.label: Action plan
planningFrame.guidance: Present an accurate one-page results brief celebrating skill acquisition and 40% referral reduction while rescheduling morning sessions around late buses and adding classroom generalization practice.

planningFrame.label: Follow-up & ethics
planningFrame.guidance: Report only de-identified aggregate and subgroup trends, avoid fabricating causality to please leadership, and connect the 6 non-improving students to Tier 3 check-ins or FBA collaboration.

successCriteria: Accurately categorizes enrollment/attendance (participation), vignette knowledge and satisfaction (Mindsets & Behaviors), and discipline referrals (outcome data).
Politely declines the principal's request to claim the 10-student group caused the school's 12 percent building-wide referral drop, citing scale, confounders, and lack of a comparison design.
Diagnoses both the knowledge-to-behavior transfer gap (8 knew steps yet only 4 dropped referrals) and the bus-tardiness attendance barrier affecting 2 students.
Recommends targeted program adaptations (rescheduling past morning arrival, in-vivo role-play/teacher prompting, and Tier 3 escalation) while preserving student privacy.
commonPitfalls: Agreeing to present the 12 percent schoolwide referral drop as proof of small-group efficacy to secure administrative goodwill.
Highlighting the 90 percent enjoyment rating as primary evidence of intervention effectiveness while downplaying unchanged or rising referrals.
Scrapping the entire conflict-resolution curriculum without first examining dosage loss from bus tardiness and classroom generalization gaps.
Including individual students' names or identifiable discipline counts in a general faculty or stakeholder results summary.
sampleOutline: Data taxonomy: Separate participation (10 students; 2 with 50% attendance), Mindsets & Behaviors (8/10 step recall; 9/10 enjoyment), and outcome data (4 reduced referrals, 4 flat, 2 increased).
Causal integrity: Inform the principal transparently that a 10-student group cannot establish causation for a schoolwide 12% drop due to scale and concurrent building factors.

Root-cause refinement: Move group timing away from late-bus arrivals, shift from verbal vignettes to active role-play and teacher cueing, and refer non-improving students for individualized Tier 3 support.
Results reporting: Deliver a concise, de-identified ASCA Small-Group Results Report pairing honest outcomes with next-cycle improvement steps.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: Postsecondary readiness advising and systemic barrier advocacy
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Remove Gatekeeping Barriers in Dual-Enrollment and Postsecondary Advising
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Combine student-centered postsecondary/career advising for a junior with an IEP and systemic equity advocacy to dismantle exclusionary dual-enrollment and financial-aid access barriers.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: An annual audit shows 41 percent of juniors qualify by GPA for dual-enrollment or AP classes, yet only 16 percent of first-generation students and 12 percent of students with IEPs enroll, amid an unwritten teacher-signature rule and an English-only 6:00 PM FAFSA night. Junior Carlos (IEP for written expression, strong in automotive diagnostics) says nobody explained apprenticeships, technical colleges, or college accommodation rules.
taskParts: Outline an individualized postsecondary and career advising plan for Carlos that leverages his automotive diagnostics strengths, IEP transition planning, and disability-support differences after high school.

Identify the systemic institutional barriers (unwritten teacher-signature policy, English-only evening FAFSA sessions, four-year-only fairs) suppressing enrollment for first-generation and IEP students.
Construct a collaborative advocacy strategy with administrators, special educators, and families to replace subjective gatekeeping with transparent, equitable postsecondary pathways.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Pair system-level gaps (41% GPA-eligible vs. 16% first-generation and 12% IEP enrollment) with Carlos's lived experience of narrow four-year advising and unaddressed IEP transition needs.

planningFrame.label: Professional framework
planningFrame.guidance: Apply ASCA Professional Standards (systemic change and advocacy), IDEA secondary transition planning, ADA/Section 504 postsecondary self-advocacy rules, and inclusive career development.

planningFrame.label: Action plan
planningFrame.guidance: Coordinate with Carlos's IEP case manager on apprenticeships and technical-college certifications while proposing objective open-enrollment criteria, multilingual FAFSA labs, and multi-pathway career fairs.

planningFrame.label: Follow-up & ethics
planningFrame.guidance: Clarify that IDEA IEPs do not transfer directly to colleges (students self-disclose to disability services under ADA/504), protect student autonomy, and audit next-year disaggregated enrollment.

successCriteria: Centers Carlos's strengths in automotive diagnostics by exploring registered apprenticeships, industry certifications, and technical colleges alongside two- and four-year options.

Explains the legal transition from IDEA (school-initiated IEP services) to postsecondary ADA/Section 504 (student self-disclosure and documentation to disability services) and links advising to his IEP transition plan.
Challenges the unwritten teacher-signature policy with disaggregated data (41% eligible vs. 16% first-generation and 12% IEP) and proposes objective, transparent course-access criteria.
Redesigns family financial-aid outreach with multilingual interpreters, varied schedules, and hands-on FAFSA completion labs rather than a single English-only evening lecture.
commonPitfalls: Steering Carlos away from rigorous dual-enrollment or technical-college pathways because of his written-expression IEP.
Telling Carlos his high school IEP automatically transfers to a technical college without explaining self-disclosure and documentation requirements under ADA/Section 504.
Advising Carlos individually while leaving the unwritten teacher-signature barrier and English-only FAFSA model untouched.
Equating postsecondary readiness exclusively with four-year university admission rather than affirming apprenticeships and skilled career credentials.
sampleOutline: Individualized career & transition advising: Partner with Carlos and his IEP team to map automotive apprenticeship, technical-college, and dual-enrollment CTE routes aligned to his strengths and goals.
Postsecondary disability literacy: Prepare Carlos to use his Summary of Performance and self-advocate with postsecondary disability services (ADA/504) since IDEA IEPs end at graduation.

Systemic barrier removal: Present the 41% vs. 16%/12% enrollment disparity to leadership to abolish unwritten teacher signatures in favor of transparent criteria and opt-out advanced course notification.

Accessible family & career ecosystems: Expand fairs to include trades/apprenticeships and host multilingual FAFSA workshops across daytime, evening, and virtual slots, tracking next-year enrollment equity.
