quickReference.title: ASCA Define Standards, Development & Ethical/Legal Duties
quickReference.purpose: Anchors ASCA Define standards, appropriate role boundaries, developmental frameworks, mandated reporting, and STEPS ethical reasoning.
checklist: Distinguish ASCA-appropriate counseling responsibilities from inappropriate administrative duties (testing coordination, discipline, master scheduling, or long-term therapy).
Apply developmental stage (Piaget, Erikson, Vygotsky) and family-systems dynamics when framing student behavior and caregiver communication.
Check confidentiality limits (foreseeable harm, mandated abuse reporting, court order) and walk through Stone's STEPS model before resolving ethical dilemmas.
formulas: ASCA Define standards (4th Ed.): ASCA Student Standards (Mindsets & Behaviors across Academic, Career, and Social/Emotional domains), Professional Standards & Competencies, and ASCA Ethical Standards (2022).

Developmental anchors: Piaget (concrete 7 to 11, formal 12+), Erikson (Industry vs Inferiority elementary; Identity vs Role Confusion adolescence), Vygotsky (ZPD scaffolding), and family systems (boundaries, triangulation).

Confidentiality and federal protections: break confidentiality for serious/foreseeable harm, suspected abuse/neglect (mandated report directly to CPS), or valid court order; McKinney-Vento guarantees immediate enrollment for unhoused youth; PPRA governs sensitive student surveys.

STEPS ethical model (Stone): define problem, check ASCA Ethics and law, weigh developmental level and parent/student rights, apply ethical principles (autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, fidelity), evaluate options, consult, and act.
decisionRules: When a student discloses suspected physical abuse or neglect at home → prioritize filing a direct mandated CPS report immediately per state law rather than investigating facts or waiting for administrative approval.

When an administrator assigns the school counselor to coordinate state testing or administer student discipline → prioritize advocating with ASCA role data to reassign non-counseling duties and protect direct student-service time.

When a parent demands all counseling session details for a non-suicidal adolescent → prioritize balancing parental legal rights with student trust by sharing general themes or inviting joint conversation unless serious foreseeable harm exists.

When an unhoused family arrives without immunization records or proof of residency → prioritize immediate enrollment and school-of-origin coordination under McKinney-Vento with the district homeless liaison.
cautions: Never promise absolute, unconditional confidentiality to a student; explain clear, developmentally appropriate limits at the start of counseling.
Do not conduct forensic abuse interviews or interrogate suspected perpetrators before reporting reasonable suspicion to Child Protective Services.
Avoid stepping into dual relationships (such as acting as disciplinarian or providing ongoing private clinical psychotherapy) that erode student trust and exceed school counseling scope.

quickReference.title: Direct/Indirect Delivery, Brief Counseling, Career & Groups
quickReference.purpose: Anchors the ASCA 80/20 delivery split, brief counseling frameworks, career theories, group screening norms, and external referral boundaries.
checklist: Verify whether the student need calls for Direct services (instruction, appraisal/advisement, short-term counseling) or Indirect services (consultation, collaboration, referral).
Screen prospective small-group members for readiness, obtain parental consent per policy, and clarify that peer confidentiality is expected but cannot be guaranteed.
Offer multiple vetted community providers (typically three or more options) whenever referring a student beyond short-term school counseling scope.
formulas: ASCA Deliver 80/20 allocation: devote at least 80% of counselor time to Direct (Instruction, Appraisal/Advisement, short-term Counseling) and Indirect (Consultation, Collaboration, Referrals) student services, and at most 20% to program planning/school support.

Brief school-counseling toolkits: SFBC (Miracle, Scaling, Exception questions), CBT/REBT (cognitive reframing and coping), Reality Therapy (WDEP: Wants, Doing, Evaluation, Plan), and Motivational Interviewing (OARS).

Career-theory anchors: Holland RIASEC (person-environment congruence), Super (Life-Span stages and self-concept), Gottfredson (Circumscription and Compromise), Krumboltz (Planned Happenstance), and SCCT (self-efficacy and outcome expectations).

Small-group guidelines: pre-group screening and consent, typically 4 to 6 elementary or 6 to 8 secondary members for 6 to 8 structured sessions moving through Forming, Storming/Transition, Norming/Working, and Termination stages.
decisionRules: When a student needs rapid, goal-directed support for test anxiety or attendance within limited school sessions → prioritize brief Solution-Focused (SFBC) or CBT coping strategies tied to Mindsets & Behaviors.

When a student exhibits persistent trauma symptoms, severe eating-disorder behaviors, or long-term psychiatric needs → prioritize family consultation and a multi-option external clinical referral rather than ongoing school psychotherapy.

When an adolescent prematurely rules out STEM careers due to gender stereotypes → prioritize Gottfredson circumscription/compromise reflection, SCCT self-efficacy building, and broad career exploration.
When a student displays disruptive aggression or acute personal crisis during group screening → prioritize individual support first rather than placing the student in a psychoeducational peer group.
cautions: Never provide long-term intensive clinical therapy inside a school counseling program, as it violates ASCA role boundaries and displaces universal and targeted student access.
Do not refer families to a single private practitioner or accept referral fees, which creates an unethical conflict of interest under ASCA Ethical Standards.
Avoid conducting classroom counseling lessons without linking objectives to specific ASCA Mindsets & Behaviors standards and measurable pre/post student data.

quickReference.title: ASCA Manage Tools, SMART Goals, Data Types & Advisory Councils
quickReference.purpose: Anchors ASCA Manage planning artifacts, 4th-Edition data categories, administrative conference timelines, and closing-the-gap design.
checklist: Disaggregate school achievement, attendance, and discipline data by subgroup before drafting Annual Student Outcome Goals or Closing-the-Gap Action Plans.
Align program beliefs, vision, and mission directly to the school and district improvement plans before selecting classroom or group interventions.
Complete the Annual Administrative Conference early in the year and convene a diverse Advisory Council at least twice annually.
formulas: ASCA 4th-Edition data triad: Participation Data (who/how many/how often), Mindsets & Behaviors Data (pre/post Attitudes, Skills, Knowledge changes), and Outcome Data (measurable shifts in achievement, attendance, or discipline).

Program Planning benchmarks: ASCA recommended caseload ratio is 250:1; Annual Administrative Conference signed with principal within the first 2 months of the school year; Advisory Council meets at least twice yearly (fall and spring).

Use-of-Time tracking: log at least two representative weeks per year (one fall, one spring) to verify at least 80% Direct/Indirect student services and no more than 20% Program Planning & School Support.

Action-plan architecture: Classroom & Group Mindsets & Behaviors Action Plan anchors universal/targeted lessons, while the Closing-the-Gap Action Plan targets specific disaggregated equity gaps with SMART outcome metrics.
decisionRules: When disaggregated data reveal significantly higher chronic absenteeism among multilingual ninth graders → prioritize a Closing-the-Gap Action Plan with a SMART attendance outcome goal rather than a generic schoolwide assembly.

When use-of-time logs show 38% of hours spent on clerical scheduling and lunch duty → prioritize bringing the data to the Annual Administrative Conference to renegotiate alignment toward the 80/20 standard.

When planning a school counseling Advisory Council → prioritize recruiting balanced representation (parents, students, teachers, administrators, community partners) to review data and advise on goals twice yearly.

When writing an Annual Student Outcome Goal → prioritize linking a specific baseline metric, target student group, measurable percentage/rate change, and timeframe directly to achievement, attendance, or discipline.
cautions: Never rely solely on Participation Data (headcounts of students served) to prove program effectiveness; stakeholders need Mindsets & Behaviors plus Outcome Data.
Do not omit the Annual Administrative Conference or leave counselor duties informal, because undocumented expectations invite inappropriate non-counseling tasks.
Avoid building an Advisory Council composed only of school staff or rubber-stamping past activities instead of sharing disaggregated goals and outcomes.

quickReference.title: Program Assessment, Results Analysis & Data-Based Advocacy
quickReference.purpose: Anchors ASCA Assess reports, counselor-specific appraisal standards, percent-change/disaggregation analysis, and systemic equity advocacy.
checklist: Evaluate every intervention across all three data layers (Participation, Mindsets & Behaviors, and Outcome) before deciding whether to sustain, revise, or replace it.
Suppress small subgroup cell counts and strip student identifiers to uphold FERPA privacy whenever publishing results reports.
Ensure counselor performance appraisal uses ASCA counselor-specific competencies rather than an unrelated classroom-teacher observation tool.
formulas: ASCA Assess instruments: School Counseling Program Assessment, Classroom & Group Results Report, Closing-the-Gap Results Report, Professional Standards & Competencies Self-Assessment, and counselor-specific Performance Appraisal.

Data analysis formulas: percent change equals ((Post minus Pre) divided by Pre) times 100; distinguish percentage-point shifts from relative percent change, and always disaggregate averages by race, gender, ELL, SES, and IEP/504 status.

Formative vs summative review: monitor Mindsets & Behaviors mid-intervention to adjust delivery formatively, and synthesize Outcome Data at cycle end to guide next year's Action Plans and RAMP alignment (5-year designation).

Continuous-improvement decision matrix: high Mindsets & Behaviors gain plus positive Outcome shift supports scaling; high Mindsets & Behaviors gain without Outcome shift flags environmental/systemic barriers needing advocacy.
decisionRules: When a Closing-the-Gap group shows strong pre/post Mindsets & Behaviors gains but no reduction in office discipline referrals → prioritize examining classroom/systemic referral bias and teacher consultation rather than blaming student motivation.

When schoolwide graduation rates look strong at 92% but disaggregated data reveal a 71% rate for students with disabilities → prioritize presenting disaggregated results to leadership and launching targeted systemic advocacy.

When an administrator evaluates a school counselor using a standard classroom-teaching rubric → prioritize advocating with ASCA Performance Appraisal templates aligned to actual school counseling duties.

When preparing an end-of-year results presentation for the school board and Advisory Council → prioritize clear visual summaries of Participation, Mindsets & Behaviors, and Outcome Data with next-year action implications and FERPA-safe aggregation.
cautions: Never report disaggregated subgroup outcomes with tiny cell counts that allow readers to identify individual students in violation of FERPA.
Do not claim direct single-cause proof from non-experimental school outcome shifts; state that counseling interventions contributed to observed gains alongside school supports.
Avoid archiving annual results reports without translating findings into concrete modifications for the next school year's goals, lessons, and systemic equity priorities.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Mismanaging confidentiality limits, mandated reporting, and FERPA record boundaries
misconceptionFamilies.description: Test-takers frequently either promise absolute secrecy to minors despite abuse or imminent-harm disclosures, wait for principal permission before calling CPS, or violate FERPA by over-sharing counseling details or storing identifiable student notes on personal cloud drives.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Explain confidentiality limits developmentally upfront, report suspected abuse/neglect directly to CPS immediately without investigating or waiting for administrative approval, break confidentiality strictly on a need-to-know basis for foreseeable serious harm, and keep sole-possession notes separate and secure from FERPA educational records.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Conflating participation, Mindsets & Behaviors, and outcome data or overclaiming causality
misconceptionFamilies.description: Candidates regularly mistake headcounts (participation data) or pre/post skill checks (Mindsets & Behaviors data) for attendance, behavior, or achievement outcome data—or claim a counseling group caused improvement without baseline trends, fidelity checks, or experimental control.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Classify every metric into the exact ASCA data tier—Participation (who/how many/how long), Mindsets & Behaviors (attitudes, knowledge, skills), or Outcome (achievement, attendance, discipline)—and pair baseline comparison, implementation fidelity, and correlational wording rather than causal overclaims.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Accepting inappropriate non-counseling duties instead of protecting the ASCA 80/20 allocation
misconceptionFamilies.description: Test-takers often either comply silently with inappropriate administrative duties (standardized test coordination, master scheduling, discipline) or refuse antagonistically instead of using ASCA Use-of-Time data and the Annual Administrative Conference to realign toward 80% direct/indirect student services.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Document actual time allocation with Use-of-Time logs, bring disaggregated student-outcome impact data to the Annual Administrative Conference, and collaboratively negotiate reassignment of non-counseling duties to protect the ASCA 80% direct/indirect and 20% program-planning benchmark.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Failing immediate supervision, structured risk screening, or parent notification in suicide crises
misconceptionFamilies.description: Candidates frequently select unsafe crisis shortcuts—sending a student expressing suicidal ideation back to class alone, relying on discredited no-harm contracts, delaying parent notification, or providing ongoing clinical therapy beyond the school counselor brief-support role.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Never leave a student at suicide risk unsupervised; conduct structured district-approved risk screening, collaborate on a safety plan (not a no-harm contract), notify parents/guardians (or CPS/emergency services if parent contact increases danger), and execute a documented warm handoff to community mental-health care.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Skipping small-group screening, informed consent, or confidentiality norms
misconceptionFamilies.description: Test-takers commonly place students into small counseling groups based on unscreened teacher nominations, blur Tier 1 classroom instruction with Tier 2 small-group intervention, skip parent/guardian consent requirements, or promise members that peers will keep everything confidential.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Use data to match Tier 1 (classroom) vs Tier 2 (targeted small group), conduct individual pre-group screening for fit and readiness, secure parent/guardian informed consent per policy, and establish explicit group norms explaining that peer confidentiality is encouraged but cannot be guaranteed.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Defaulting to individual student deficit framing instead of systemic equity advocacy
misconceptionFamilies.description: Candidates frequently respond to racial, linguistic, or socioeconomic gaps in discipline, course access, or attendance by trying to "fix" individual students or celebrating schoolwide averages that mask persistent subgroup disparities.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Disaggregate achievement, attendance, discipline, and access data by student subgroups to pinpoint systemic barriers, engage stakeholders to examine inequitable policies or gatekeeping practices, and build measurable closing-the-gap action plans.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Mismanaging confidentiality limits, mandated reporting, and FERPA record boundaries
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Hold strict confidentiality except for mandated safety duties and FERPA rules
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: The chosen answer delays a CPS report to consult an administrator, investigates abuse personally, shares private session details casually, or saves identifiable student notes in a personal cloud account.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does this situation trigger a legal exception to confidentiality (suspected abuse/neglect or foreseeable serious harm), and how must student records be protected under FERPA and ASCA standards?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Inspect the ethical dilemma and flag whether your original response erred toward improper secrecy (failing to report abuse/harm) or improper disclosure/storage (violating FERPA or personal-cloud security).
stages.requiredOutput: Identify the exact ASCA Ethical Standard or FERPA boundary crossed by your initial choice.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: State the dual ethical rule: (1) mandated reporting of suspected child abuse/neglect goes directly to CPS without waiting for principal permission or conducting a forensic investigation, and duty to warn/protect discloses only minimum necessary details when foreseeable serious harm exists; (2) under FERPA, educational records belong in secured district systems while sole-possession memory-aid notes remain strictly private and never live in unsecured personal cloud accounts.
stages.requiredOutput: Write the exact reporting or record-security sequence required by the scenario, including transparent student notification when safe.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Resolve two ethical scenarios: (1) a fifth grader discloses bruises inflicted by a caregiver and begs you not to tell anyone, while the assistant principal asks you to wait until she calls the caregiver first; and (2) a counselor uploads identifiable student counseling notes to a personal cloud folder to work from home.
stages.requiredOutput: Specify immediate direct CPS reporting (without calling the suspected perpetrator) in Scenario 1 and district-secured FERPA-compliant record storage in Scenario 2.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Retry the missed ethics item and transfer the confidentiality boundary to a teacher asking for full details from a student individual counseling session.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the ASCA-compliant action and explain how to support classroom collaboration through need-to-know functional strategies without disclosing confidential session content.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Conflating participation, Mindsets & Behaviors, and outcome data or overclaiming causality
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Separate participation, Mindsets & Behaviors, and outcome data before claiming impact
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: The chosen answer cites session attendance counts or a skill post-test as an achievement/attendance outcome, ignores missing fidelity when results are flat, or claims a non-randomized group caused higher graduation.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Which ASCA data tier does this measure represent (Participation, Mindsets & Behaviors, or Outcome), were sessions delivered with fidelity, and does the design support association rather than causation?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Examine the data statement in the vignette and identify whether your chosen answer mislabeled an ASCA data tier, overlooked uncompleted sessions, or endorsed a causal claim from observational data.
stages.requiredOutput: Name the exact data-interpretation fallacy present in the distractor (tier confusion, missing baseline/fidelity check, leading survey item, or correlation-as-causation).

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Sort all three ASCA National Model data tiers: Participation (number of students, sessions, minutes), Mindsets & Behaviors (pre/post attitude, knowledge, or demonstrated skill checks), and Outcome (measurable shifts in achievement, attendance, or discipline)—and verify baseline data, implementation fidelity, unbiased survey wording, and correlational language in results reports.
stages.requiredOutput: Write one concrete example of Participation, Mindsets & Behaviors, and Outcome data for a single ninth-grade transition intervention.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Audit two program-evaluation findings: (1) a lesson series shows zero improvement in tardies, but logs reveal only 3 of 6 lessons were delivered, and (2) a counselor results report states that a study-skills group "caused" a 14% rise in passing grades because group participants outperformed non-participants.
stages.requiredOutput: Diagnose Finding 1 as an implementation-fidelity failure (not proof the curriculum failed) and rewrite Finding 2 using accurate pre/post association language.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-answer the missed Manage or Assess item and transfer the evaluation rigor to reconciling three conflicting data sources on school belonging.
stages.requiredOutput: Choose the methodologically sound evaluation action and explain how triangulating baseline, fidelity, and subgroup data guides program improvement.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Accepting inappropriate non-counseling duties instead of protecting the ASCA 80/20 allocation
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Apply Use-of-Time data and the Annual Conference to defend 80/20 services
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: The chosen answer passively absorbs full-time testing coordination or discipline duty, or refuses an administrator without offering Use-of-Time evidence and collaborative solutions.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Is this assigned task an appropriate counseling role or an inappropriate non-counseling duty, and how do Use-of-Time data and the Annual Administrative Conference protect the ASCA 80/20 balance?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Classify the assigned duty in the vignette against the ASCA Appropriate vs Inappropriate Activities list and note whether your original choice fell into passive compliance or unproductive confrontation.
stages.requiredOutput: Label the task as direct student service, indirect student service, program planning/school support (≤20%), or inappropriate non-counseling duty.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Follow the ASCA collaborative advocacy sequence: track actual hours via a Use-of-Time assessment → show how non-counseling duties displace direct/indirect student services needed for annual student outcome goals → bring data and a feasible transition plan to the Annual Administrative Conference (and advisory council if systemic) to restore the 80% direct/indirect / 20% planning-support target.
stages.requiredOutput: Draft a concise 3-step talking frame pairing Use-of-Time numbers with student achievement, attendance, or mental-health impact.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Respond to two staffing assignments: (1) a principal assigns the school counselor to coordinate all state standardized testing logistics for three weeks during spring transition planning, and (2) weekly calendar logs show only 52% direct/indirect student services due to lunchroom supervision and clerical schedule entry.
stages.requiredOutput: Specify the data-driven collaborative advocacy move for Assignment 1 and the Annual Administrative Conference realignment proposal for Assignment 2.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Retry the missed Define or Manage item and transfer role-clarity principles to addressing counselor burnout and maintaining alignment between the program mission and the school educational mission.
stages.requiredOutput: Confirm the ASCA-aligned response and explain why linking role advocacy to student outcomes persuades administrators better than personal complaints.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Failing immediate supervision, structured risk screening, or parent notification in suicide crises
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Maintain continuous supervision, structured screening, and caregiver handoff in suicide crises
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: The chosen answer allows a student with suicidal ideation to return to class alone, relies on a no-harm contract, delays parent notification, or initiates long-term clinical therapy in school.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Is the student under continuous adult supervision right now, has structured risk screening and collaborative safety planning occurred, and have parents/guardians and clinical referrals been activated?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Scan the crisis stem for immediate safety gaps—unsupervised movement, reliance on a verbal promise or no-harm contract, delayed parent notification, or scope-of-practice overreach into ongoing psychotherapy.
stages.requiredOutput: Pinpoint the specific safety lapse or role-boundary error in your initial answer choice.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Lock in the non-negotiable suicide-response sequence: (1) maintain continuous line-of-sight adult supervision—never leave the student alone; (2) conduct a district-approved structured risk screen (ideation, intent, plan, means, prior attempts, protective factors); (3) notify parents/guardians promptly (unless parent involvement threatens safety, then contact CPS/emergency responders); (4) build a collaborative safety plan rather than a no-harm contract; and (5) document actions and provide warm-handoff referrals to community mental-health clinicians with a school re-entry plan.
stages.requiredOutput: List the exact ordered steps from disclosure to safe release/transfer and state why no-harm contracts are contraindicated.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Manage two urgent scenarios: (1) a tenth grader tells you they have a plan to end their life tonight and asks to go back to fourth-period math to grab their backpack while you call home; and (2) after emergency hospitalization, a caregiver asks the school counselor to provide weekly long-term trauma therapy.
stages.requiredOutput: Write the immediate supervision + parent-notification protocol for Scenario 1 and the brief school-support + community-referral boundary response for Scenario 2.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-solve the missed Deliver or ethics item and transfer the scope-of-practice boundary to distinguishing short-term solution-focused school counseling from external clinical treatment.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the safest, ASCA-compliant action and justify why immediate supervision and caregiver/community linkage supersede routine confidentiality.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Skipping small-group screening, informed consent, or confidentiality norms
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Screen members, secure consent, and set realistic group confidentiality norms
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: The chosen answer enrolls students into a small group without pre-screening, uses small groups for a grade-wide need better served in Tier 1, skips parent consent, or guarantees peer secrecy.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does data call for Tier 1 classroom lessons or a Tier 2 small group, has every member been individually screened with appropriate consent, and do norms clarify that peer confidentiality cannot be guaranteed?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Review the group-counseling or tiered-delivery stem to see whether your initial answer skipped member screening, mismatched Tier 1 vs Tier 2 delivery, omitted informed consent, or overpromised confidentiality.
stages.requiredOutput: Name the exact ethical or group-design step omitted in your original choice.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Map the ASCA group-counseling checklist: use school data to decide Tier 1 (most students need the skill → classroom instruction) vs Tier 2 (targeted subgroup → 4–8 week small group); screen each candidate individually for topic fit, readiness, and exclusion of acute crisis or incompatible dynamics; obtain parent/guardian informed consent per district policy; and teach group norms stating that the counselor maintains confidentiality within legal limits but cannot guarantee peers will keep disclosures private.
stages.requiredOutput: Specify the screening criterion, consent step, and confidentiality disclaimer required before Session 1 begins.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Design tiered delivery for two situations: (1) grade-level data show 75% of sixth graders struggle with planner organization while 8 students also show severe test anxiety; and (2) during screening for a grief group, one student discloses active suicidal ideation.
stages.requiredOutput: Assign Tier 1 classroom lessons vs Tier 2 small group cleanly in Situation 1, and explain why the student in Situation 2 is excluded from the group for immediate individual crisis intervention and referral.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-answer the missed Deliver item and transfer the developmental-fit standard to choosing age-appropriate career exploration activities (awareness in elementary vs exploration in middle vs postsecondary planning in high school).
stages.requiredOutput: Defend the correct tiered/group decision by citing member screening, consent, realistic confidentiality norms, and measurable group goals.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Defaulting to individual student deficit framing instead of systemic equity advocacy
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Disaggregate data to dismantle systemic barriers instead of blaming students
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: The chosen answer tells struggling or underrepresented students to work harder, celebrates aggregate gains that hide subgroup gaps, or treats a systemic policy disparity as an individual counseling issue.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: What do disaggregated subgroup data reveal about institutional policies, access barriers, or low survey reach—and what systemic advocacy move closes the gap?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Inspect the equity scenario and check whether your original answer focused solely on fixing an individual student mindset or relied on a schoolwide average that concealed an underserved subgroup gap.
stages.requiredOutput: Identify the deficit-framing assumption or aggregate-data blind spot in your initial choice.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Apply the ASCA systemic-change lens: disaggregate achievement, attendance, discipline, course-enrollment, and survey-response data by race/ethnicity, language status, disability, and socioeconomic indicators; examine policies, prerequisites, and scheduling barriers driving disparities; partner with teachers, administrators, families, and the advisory council; and launch a measurable closing-the-gap action plan.
stages.requiredOutput: State the exact data disaggregation check and one policy- or practice-level advocacy move that addresses the root barrier.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Respond to two equity reports: (1) schoolwide attendance rose 4% after an incentive campaign, but multilingual-learner attendance declined 6%; and (2) an annual parent needs survey shows strong satisfaction overall, yet responses came from fewer than 10% of families in two neighborhood feeders.
stages.requiredOutput: Specify root-cause subgroup inquiry and barrier removal for Report 1 and multilingual/accessible outreach to correct non-response bias in Report 2.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Retry the missed Define or Assess item and transfer the equity lens to reviewing ninth-grade course-placement prerequisites that disproportionately track first-generation students out of college-preparatory pathways.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the systemic-advocacy option and explain how disaggregated outcome tracking holds the school counseling program accountable for equitable results.
